title: Additive-error exponent of linear-size spanners
formal: For every fixed real edge-budget coefficient \(c\ge1\), determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:A_c(n)+1=O_c(n^a)\text{ as }n\to\infty\}.\] Here \(A_c(n)\), defined below, is the largest, over simple undirected unweighted \(n\)-vertex graphs, minimum additive all-pairs distance error of a spanning subgraph with at most \(\lfloor cn\rfloor\) edges and the same connected components. The edge budget is genuinely linear; no hidden logarithmic factor in the budget is allowed.
why: The linear edge regime compresses a graph to a constant number of retained edges per vertex. Determining its unavoidable distance loss would quantify a fundamental limit on how accurately arbitrary graph metrics can survive such strong sparsification.
status_note: The survey leaves the linear-size error tradeoff open. The later lower-bound and nearly linear upper-bound abstracts were checked on 13 September 2026 and do not give matching bounds for every fixed linear coefficient. No full determination was verified; status remains source_open.
review_note: Completed individual source and formulation review on 13 September 2026; see statement_review and research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The survey explicitly asks for the optimal additive error achievable with a linear number of edges.
The later paper proves an \(\Omega(n^{1/7})\) lower bound in the linear-edge regime.
The subsequent upper-bound abstract reports \(O(n^{0.403})\) error with \(\widetilde O(n)\) edges, a distinct edge budget from the strict linear target.

sentences: A sparse subgraph can increase distances even when all connected components are preserved.
The card fixes a constant multiple of the vertex count as the edge budget.
It asks for the exponent of the smallest worst-case additive distance error.
Every fixed budget coefficient has an answer to absolute accuracy 0.01.
New edges and hidden logarithmic increases in the edge budget are not allowed.

definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target. Define the exponent \[x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)=\inf\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \exists n_0\ge1\ \forall n\ge n_0,\ A_c(n)+1\le Cn^a\}.\] For each fixed real \(c\ge1\), the constants may depend on \(c\) and \(a\), but not on the graph or \(n\). Adding one removes zero-value conventions without changing any positive power of growth. A spanning forest has finite distances at most \(n-1\) within its components, so \(0\le x_{\mathrm{span}}(c)\le1\). The infimum need not be attained; no ordinary logarithmic-growth limit is assumed. In particular, exponent zero permits polylogarithmic or other subpolynomial error and does not promise bounded error.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s Section 8.4, item 3, asks how much additive error is unavoidable with \(O(n)\) retained edges. Its dated bounds leave a polynomial gap between what sparse subgraphs can achieve and what some input metrics force.

Bodwin and Hoppenworth subsequently establish an \(\Omega(n^{1/7})\) additive-error lower bound for linear-size spanners, improving the lower bound quoted in the survey. This is a lower bound, not a matching determination.

The later Almost-Optimal Sublinear Additive Spanners abstract reports \(O(n^{0.403})\) additive error with \(\widetilde O(n)\) edges. That edge budget hides logarithmic factors and cannot be substituted for a fixed \(cn\) budget in this question.

answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real answer \(a(c)\) for every real \(c\ge1\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of absolute error at most \(1/100\) in the defined exponent. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. Both sides of the interval must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. The infimum need not be attained, and no ordinary logarithmic growth limit is assumed. Matching logarithmic factors, leading constants and an algorithm attaining the endpoint exponent are not required. A one-sided improvement alone qualifies only if the resulting certified interval is sufficiently narrow.
